title: Double seronegative myasthenia gravis with antiphospholipid syndrome: a case report
case_prompt: A 42-year-old Caucasian woman was admitted for fluctuating diplopia, ptosis, dysphagia, dysarthria, and fatigable chewing at the end of meals or at the end of the day. Her medical history included antiphospholipid syndrome, with three spontaneous abortions, and transient hypothyroidism. She took aspirin 81 mg daily. On examination, she had dysarthria and weakness of the facial muscles, tongue, and neck, and displayed progressive fatigability in upward gaze during the Simpson test. Repetitive ulnar nerve stimulation showed an abnormal (>10%) decrement. Tests for antibodies against AChR, MuSK, and titin were negative. A thoracic computed tomography scan was normal. Thromboplastin time and activated partial thromboplastin time were elevated; anticardiolipin and anti–β2-glycoprotein-I antibodies were elevated, consistent with her antiphospholipid syndrome.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. The presence of fatigable ocular and bulbar muscle weakness with an abnormal decrement on repetitive nerve stimulation supports a diagnosis of myasthenia gravis — “Repetitive ulnar nerve stimulation showed abnormal (>10%) decrement.”  
2. The absence of antibodies against AChR, MuSK, and titin despite clinical and electrophysiologic findings indicates seronegative myasthenia gravis — “The results of tests to detect antibodies against AChR, MuSK and titin were negative.”  
3. The normal thoracic computed tomography scan excludes a thymoma-associated form of myasthenia gravis — “Her thoracic computed tomography scan was normal.”
